newsitem.title: RUSSIA: SOCCER-OLD FAVOURITES TO DOMINATE NEW RUSSIAN SEASON.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-OLD FAVOURITES TO DOMINATE NEW RUSSIAN SEASON.

text.p: Russian soccer, still out of step with the rest of Europe, opens a new season on Sunday with a sprinkling of new characters but with a basic plot that looks all too familiar.

Champions Spartak Moscow, winners of four out of the five post-Soviet Russian championships, start as heavy title favourites, having succeeded in fending off west European interest in top-scoring winger Andrei Tikhonov and playmaker and captain Ilya Tsymbalar.
Revamped Torpedo Moscow and others may hope to make an impact but Spartak's main threat seems likely to come from last year's runner-up and 1995 champions, Alania Vladikavkaz.

Alania coach Valery Gazzayev, taking advantage of the Bosman ruling, has brought in more Georgians from just across the Caucasus. Georgian international Kakhi Tskhadadze and Georgian-born Russian international Akhrik Tsveiba beef up the defence following Omar Tetradze's departure for Roma.
Vladikavkaz may hope to take on the role their Georgian neighbours Dynamo Tbilisi enjoyed in Soviet days but they face mass opposition from Moscow's relatively rich "Big Five."
"For the top places, it's going to be between the five Moscow sides, Alania and Rotor (Volgograd)," Russian national coach Boris Ignatyev predictably forecast, naming last year's top seven.
Of the other Moscow sides, Dynamo are certain to be contenders as are cup holders Lokomotiv, despite the imminent departure of Russian national goalkeeper Sergei Ovchinnikov to Benfica.

A question mark hangs over army side CSKA after a bitter internal split. Torpedo-Luzhniki, rescued from the bankrupt ZiL car plant by the capital's free-spending mayor, may be a surprise package after poaching CSKA coach Alexander Tarkhanov and much of his squad during the close season.
Torpedo also field Brazilians Leonidas and Carlos and move this summer to the expensively refurbished Luzhniki stadium.

Rotor Volgograd, seemingly on course for the title last year before blowing their lead, hope to go better than third this season. Denis Zubko from Zenit St Petersburg reinforces Russia's top-scoring duo, Oleg Veretennikov and Vladimir Nidergaus.

But the season has already started badly for the club that knocked Manchester United out of last season's UEFA Cup. Rotor are among eight clubs forced to play their first two home fixtures at neutral grounds after failing to instal undersoil heating.

Second city team Zenit St Petersburg are hoping to improve on last year's 10th place under former Soviet Union coach Anatoly Byshovets, who replaced the sacked Pavel Sadyrin. Former Russia coach Sadyrin now leads CSKA.

Last year's slight pick-up in attendances and a thrilling finale that ended with Spartak edging out Alania in a play-off have fuelled hopes Russian soccer may finally be emerging from the slump that followed the collapse of the Soviet sporting machine.
But poor performances in the European club competitions -- no Russian side went beyond the second round this season -- show much remains to be done.
A drain of talent to European clubs is part of the problem but the Russians are taking steps to raise the domestic game.

The premier league will be cut to 16 teams from 18 in 1998 and may be further reduced. Tough penalties for unheated pitches are the first shots in a campaign that may end with Russian soccer playing through the winter in a calendar more in line with the rest of Europe.
